newsitem.title: USA: Texas jury declines murder charge in border killing.
newsitem.headline: Texas jury declines murder charge in border killing.

text.p: A grand jury Thursday declined to indict a U.S. Marine on murder charges for shooting dead a Texas teen-ager herding goats near the Mexican border in May.

Presidio County District Attorney Albert Valadez said no charges would be filed against Marine Cpl. Clemente Banuelos, who shot 18-year-old Esequiel Hernandez in an apparent mix-up during a military anti-narcotics operation along the border.
Hernandez was killed with a single bullet from an assault rifle as he herded his goats in remote hills near his home in the tiny Texas border town of Redford May 20.

Backed by the Pentagon, Banuelos and three other Marines who were with him on the surveillance mission said he opened fire only because Hernandez had already fired at the group and was about to do so again.

But the dead man's family said he was simply herding his goats, would never shoot at anyone and only carried an old .22 caliber rifle to scare off wild dogs. Civilian investigators had said evidence contradicted the Marines' version of events.
The death of Hernandez brought a storm of protest over the use of military forces in civilian areas to combat drug trafficking.
Valadez said a grand jury indictment would have needed the support of at least nine of the 12 jurors, but was rejected.

"They believed the Marines were telling the truth when they said Zeke (Hernandez) fired the first shot," he told reporters outside the courthouse where the grand jury met in the west Texas town of Marfa. "The grand jury believed the Marines were following the rules of engagement."
Many Redford residents believe Hernandez did not see the camouflaged Marines, and accidentally fired near them as he took target practice.

They claim military personnel should never have been sent into the area and said after the grand jury's no-bill decision Thursday that they would push for another grand jury probe and a special investigation into the case.
"It comes as no surprise to us but this is not the end, this is the beginning," said Melvin LaFollette, a member of the Redford Citizens' Committee for Justice which was set up after the shooting.
Hernandez's elder brother, Margarito, simply shook his head and said, "Nothing good, nothing good."
But Banuelos' attorney, Jack Zimmermann, said justice had been served.

"A young man could have been wrongly charged in a crime," said Zimmermann, a colorful Houston-based lawyer who wore light tan cowboy boots and a cowboy hat here Thursday. "This is a night that makes me proud to be a Texan."
Banuelos, who is from California, could still face a civil lawsuit filed by Hernandez's family.

After the shooting, the Defense Department suspended all anti-narcotics patrols of the type that Banuelos had been on, pending a review of whether U.S. armed forces should be involved in such efforts to stop cocaine and other drugs from being smuggled across the Mexican border.
But the Pentagon strongly defended Banuelos earlier Thursday.
"We don't think an indictment is justified based on what we know," Defense Department spokesman Ken Bacon told a news briefing.

"He (Banuelos) was performing appropriately as a member of the armed services in defense of the national interest. He followed the rules of engagement clearly. And those rules of engagement allowed him to defend himself," Bacon said. "And he was under fire; he and his three other Marines were under fire. And (Banuelos) acted appropriately in self-defense."
An attorney for one of the other Marines earlier said the men had radioed to superiors after Hernandez fired a shot at them and they were told to return fire if targeted again.
All of the Marines except Banuelos appeared before the grand jury and testified on his behalf.
"He saved my life and I don't think at all he should be charged. I would do the same for him," Lance Cpl. James Blood told reporters, adding that he and the others regretted Hernandez's death.
"I feel sorry for the family. If there was something i could do to fix it, I would," he said.
Blood and the other two Marines could have faced conspiracy charges but also escaped indictments.
